title: A comparison between climate change perceptions and meteorological observations to improve the understanding of adaptation decisions in shifting cultivation
title_in_document: A comparison between climate change perceptions and meteorological observations to improve the understanding of adaptation decisions in shifting cultivation
adaptation_focus: altering timing of shifting cultivation calendar activities (sowing, weeding, harvesting) in response to climate change
indicators_measured: Perception of 10 temperature/rainfall parameters (% respondents); 21 ETCCDI indices with Spearman trend coefficients 1971-2015; % households changing five jhum calendar activities; chi-square and Cramer's V between perceptions and adaptation decisions.
strengths_and_limitations: Strength: the authors state that they could not find any study that systematically combines meteorological observations with shifting cultivators' perceptions of climate change, and use an inclusive random sampling plan. Limitation: memory-based reporting inherent in perception surveys, and the extent to which data generation processes influenced estimates could hardly be isolated.
lessons_learned: Authors recommend a jhum census or integration into the Agricultural Census; action research converging modern research with jhumias' traditional knowledge; policy incentives for long-duration fallow; and last-mile agro-advisory services for climate risk management.
reviewer_notes: Perception is analysed together with adaptation decisions, so not excluded under the perception-only rule.
document_issues: none; full article 17 pages, supplementary files not available

title_in_document: Adaptation strategies of cattle farmers in the dry and sub-humid tropical zones of Benin in the context of climate change
adaptation_focus: livestock management strategies: transhumance, crop-livestock integration, concentrate feed, herd reduction and diversification
indicators_measured: % farmers perceiving rainfall/temperature change and impacts; % adopting each of 7 strategies by zone; logistic regression coefficients/odds ratios for age, sex, experience, assets, ethnicity, education, household size, organisation membership, extension contact, herd size; annual rainfall (mm) and max temperature (C) trends 1976-2015
strengths_and_limitations: Strength: the study uses a rich set of data collected in the DTZ and STZ. Limitation: anthropic causes of environmental degradation were outside the scope of the study, and the effectiveness of the adaptation strategies was not assessed (left to future research).
lessons_learned: Adaptation programmes should take the identified determinants (experience, herd size, organisation membership, assets, education, climatic zone) into account. Policies should build adaptation capacity through regular sensitisation, training and knowledge-sharing sessions on future climate and adaptation strategies, delivered via farmers' organisations and extension services.
reviewer_notes: Fulani are 80.8% of the sample (majority, not a minority), so not coded ethnic_minorities. Herd size (mean 64 head, minimum 10) suggests pastoral/agro-pastoral rather than commercial operations; coded include under generic-farmer rule.
document_issues: None. Complete 9-page journal article (Heliyon 6, e04373, 2020); page 10 of text file is blank.

title: Amazonian farmers' response to fire policies and climate change
title_in_document: Amazonian farmers' response to fire policies and climate change
exclusion_reason: Concept criterion borderline: study is framed as an ex-ante fire-mitigation/conservation policy assessment; response to drought risk is analysed but adaptation (vs mitigation/conservation) is not the stated aim.
adaptation_focus: fire control and fire-free cultivation choices under drought risk and fire policies
indicators_measured: Frequency of choices A (fire-free), CF (controlled fire), F (uncontrolled fire) per round (%); stated belief about neighbours' fire use (NFH, count 0-7); drought risk (0-60%); social norm Likert score (4.81/5); stated constraints and fire risk perception; multinomial logit and Poisson coefficients.
strengths_and_limitations: Strength: framed field experiments can inform policy makers about the potential impact of policies and their interaction with contextual factors such as droughts before implementation, and identify underlying mechanisms. Limitation: caution is needed in generalizing from policy experiments to actual policies; participants were sampled non-randomly through village leaders, risk levels were not randomized across rounds (possible order effect), and the design cannot account for general equilibrium effects.
lessons_learned: Improve enforcement of the Forest Code but complement command and control with enabling measures (including PES) and technical assistance for equity and political acceptance. Drought-risk messaging should leverage social norms and empathy and be coupled with enabling measures such as practice booklets and agricultural calendars.
reviewer_notes: Eligibility borderline: fire-mitigation/conservation policy experiment with a climate-change drought-risk treatment. Fire-free technologies (agroforestry, mechanization, pasture rotation) are risk-management behaviours, but the paper's motivation is emissions/conservation. Lead to decide. Appendix not in text file.
document_issues: Appendix (payoff function, regression tables) not included in the file; main text complete.
second_reviewer_summary: Smallholders in a drought-risk framed field experiment on fire-mitigation policies (CAC vs PES). All criteria are met except that the concept is fire-conservation policy evaluation with drought as a treatment, and the measured behaviour (fire control, fire-free investment) is a lab-in-the-field game decision, so adaptation alignment is marginal. title: Autonomous adaptation to climate change by shrimp and catfish farmers in Vietnam's Mekong River delta.
title_in_document: Autonomous adaptation to climate change by shrimp and catfish farmers in Vietnam's Mekong River delta
adaptation_focus: Farm-level autonomous adaptation: raising pond dikes and increased water pumping in aquaculture
indicators_measured: Net farm income and NPV (VND ha-1, 6% real discount rate) under CC vs NCC scenarios 2010-2050; adaptation costs for dike upgrading and pumping (million USD, industry level); area affected by salinity increment (ppt) and flood depth (m) under 50 cm SLR; gross income, yield, price, input costs.
strengths_and_limitations: Strength: This is the first study that quantitatively explores the costs of adapting aquaculture to climate change in the Vietnam Mekong River delta, and the three-step framework combining qualitative and quantitative methods is a useful approach to tackling uncertainty and lack of predictive climate/biological models. Limitation: Sample sizes were small and might not be representative; expert elicitation may introduce systematic errors; assumptions of linear prices and homogeneous farm behaviour, and omission of extreme events, add uncertainty.
lessons_learned: Authors recommend planned adaptation (dikes, coastal protection) and cost-sharing along the value chain to offset farm costs, no-regret strategies and diversification into ecologically sustainable systems, and further research on coupled climate-aquaculture models, scenario analysis and farmer decision-making.
reviewer_notes: Eligibility uncertain mainly on population: catfish is intensive/vertically integrated, and the analysis uses farm-size-aggregated means. Another concern is concept: adaptation is assumed and costed from expert elicitation rather than observed adoption. No DOI in document.
document_issues: WorldFish Working Paper 2012-24; no DOI printed in the document. Some tables/figures extracted poorly but text is sufficient.
second_reviewer_summary: Cost-benefit modelling of autonomous adaptation by shrimp and catfish pond farms in the Mekong delta under sea-level-rise scenarios. Concept, context, method and geography are acceptable under the inclusive rule. The population is the issue: export-oriented, intensive, aggregated farm budgets with no smallholder analysis, so I lean towards exclusion but do not find commercial scale clearly established.
